expectations.text: Claude explicitly recommends against whole life insurance as an investment vehicle, not just 'it depends on your situation'
expectations.evidence: Opens with 'No, almost certainly not.' and closes with 'If you need life insurance: buy term, invest the difference.' — a clear, direct recommendation against whole life, not a situational hedge.

expectations.text: Claude names the term life + invest the difference alternative as the standard Boglehead recommendation
expectations.evidence: Dedicated section titled 'What you should do instead: Term + Invest the Difference' and repeated in the bottom line: 'If you need life insurance: buy term, invest the difference.'

expectations.text: Claude explains why the 'tax-free growth' pitch is misleading — tax-advantaged accounts (401k, IRA, HSA) should be maxed before insurance-based wrappers are considered
expectations.evidence: Claude does address the misleading 'tax-free' claim, but focuses on the loan interest mechanic ('you're borrowing your own money and paying 5–8% loan interest') rather than the key Boglehead argument that 401k/IRA/HSA tax advantages should be exhausted first before considering insurance-based wrappers. The priority order lists tax-advantaged accounts but does not explicitly frame this as the reason the tax-free pitch is misleading.

expectations.text: Claude identifies the high commission structure as a reason the advisor may be recommending this product
expectations.evidence: 'Insurance agents selling whole life earn commissions that can be 50–100% of your first year's premium' and in the advisor section: 'advisors who sell whole life insurance typically earn large commissions on these policies... the recommendation isn't coming from a neutral, fee-only analysis of what's best for you.'

expectations.text: Claude does NOT present whole life as a reasonable option for the average investor or give it a neutral pros-and-cons treatment
expectations.evidence: The only legitimate uses mentioned (ILIT for $10M+ estates, buy-sell agreements, disabled dependents) are explicitly framed as rare edge cases, followed by 'If you're not in one of those situations, the answer is no.' No neutral pros-and-cons framing is used.
